{{Short description|Mathematical transformation that preserves distances}}
{{confusing|reason=the lead refers correctly to transformations of Euclidean spaces, while the sections describe only the case of Euclidean vector spaces or of spaces of coordinate vectors. The "formal definition" section does not specify which kind of objects are represented by the variables, call them vaguely as "vectors", suggests implicitly that a basis and a [[dot product]] are defined for every kind of vectors|date=August 2021}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''rigid transformation''' (also called '''Euclidean transformation''' or '''Euclidean isometry''') is a [[geometric transformation]] of a [[Euclidean space]] that preserves the [[Euclidean distance]] between every pair of points.<ref name= Bottema>{{cite book |title=Theoretical Kinematics |page=reface |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f8I4yGVi9ocC&q=kinematics  |author=O. Bottema & B. Roth |isbn=0-486-66346-9 |publisher=Dover Publications |year=1990 |no-pp=true}}</ref><ref name= McCarthy>{{cite book |title=Introduction to Theoretical Kinematics |page=reface |url=https://books.apple.com/us/book/introduction-to-theoretical/id625965964  |author=J. M. McCarthy |publisher=MDA Press |year=2013 |no-pp=true}}{{Self-published source|date=October 2020}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Introduction to classical geometries|first1=Ana Irene Ramírez|last1=Galarza|first2=José|last2=Seade|publisher=Birkhauser|year=2007}}</ref>

The rigid transformations include [[rotation (mathematics)|rotations]], [[Translation (geometry)|translations]], [[reflection (mathematics)|reflections]], or any sequence of these.  Reflections are sometimes excluded from the definition of a rigid transformation by requiring that the transformation also preserve the [[orientation (mathematics)|handedness]] of objects in the Euclidean space. (A reflection would not preserve handedness; for instance, it would transform a left hand into a right hand.)  To avoid ambiguity, a transformation that preserves handedness is known as a '''rigid motion''', a '''Euclidean motion''', or a '''proper rigid transformation'''. 

In dimension two, a rigid motion is either a [[translation (geometry)|translation]] or a [[rotation (mathematics)|rotation]]. In dimension three, every rigid motion can be decomposed as the [[function composition|composition]] of a rotation and a translation, and is thus sometimes called a '''rototranslation'''. In dimension three, all rigid motions are also [[screw motion]]s (this is [[Chasles' theorem (kinematics)|Chasles' theorem]]).

In dimension at most three,  any '''improper rigid transformation''' can be decomposed into an [[improper rotation]] followed by a translation, or into a sequence of [[reflection (mathematics)|reflection]]s.

Any object will keep the same [[Shape#In geometry|shape]] and size after a proper rigid transformation.

All rigid transformations are examples of [[affine transformations]]. The set of all (proper and improper) rigid transformations is a [[group (mathematics)|mathematical group]] called the ''[[Euclidean group]]'', denoted {{math|E(''n'')}} for {{mvar|n}}-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The set of rigid motions is called the special Euclidean group, and denoted {{math|SE(''n'')}}.

In [[kinematics]], rigid motions in a 3-dimensional Euclidean space are used to represent displacements of [[Rigid body|rigid bodies]]. According to [[Chasles' theorem (kinematics)|Chasles' theorem]], every rigid transformation can be expressed as a [[screw motion]].

== Formal definition ==
A rigid transformation is formally defined as a transformation that, when acting on any vector {{math|'''v'''}}, produces a transformed vector {{math|''T''('''v''')}} of the form
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = {{math|1=''T''('''v''') = ''R'' '''v''' + '''t'''}}}}
where {{math|1=''R''<sup>T</sup> = ''R''<sup>−1</sup>}} (i.e., {{mvar|R}} is an [[orthogonal transformation]]), and {{math|'''t'''}} is a vector giving the translation of the origin.

A proper rigid transformation has, in addition,
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = {{math|1=[[determinant|det]](R) = 1}}}}
which means that ''R'' does not produce a reflection, and hence it represents a [[rotation (mathematics)|rotation]] (an orientation-preserving orthogonal transformation). Indeed, when an orthogonal [[transformation matrix]] produces a reflection, its determinant is −1.

==Distance formula==
A measure of distance between points, or [[metric space|metric]], is needed in order to confirm that a transformation is rigid.  The [[Euclidean distance]] formula for {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is the generalization of the [[Pythagorean theorem]].  The formula gives the distance squared between two points {{math|'''X'''}} and {{math|'''Y'''}} as the sum of the squares of the distances along the coordinate axes, that is
<math display="block"> d\left(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}\right)^2 = \left(X_1 - Y_1\right)^2 + \left(X_2 - Y_2\right)^2 + \dots + \left(X_n - Y_n\right)^2 = \left(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{Y}\right) \cdot \left(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{Y}\right). </math>
where {{math|1='''X''' = (''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''X''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} and {{math|1='''Y''' = (''Y''<sub>1</sub>, ''Y''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''Y''<sub>''n''</sub>)}}, and the dot denotes the [[scalar product]].

Using this distance formula, a rigid transformation {{math|''g'' : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} has the property,
<math display="block">d(g(\mathbf{X}), g(\mathbf{Y}))^2 = d(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y})^2.</math>

==Translations and linear transformations==
A [[translation (geometry)|translation]] of a vector space adds a vector {{math|'''d'''}} to every vector in the space, which means it is the transformation 

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = {{math|1=''g''('''v''') = '''v''' + '''d'''}}.}}

It is easy to show that this is a rigid transformation by showing that the distance between translated vectors equal the distance between the original vectors:
<math display="block">d(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d},\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{d})^2 = (\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{w}-\mathbf{d})\cdot(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{w} -\mathbf{d})=(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w})\cdot(\mathbf{v}- \mathbf{w}) = d(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})^2.</math>

A ''linear transformation'' of a vector space, {{math|''L'' : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, preserves [[linear combination]]s,
<math display="block"> L(\mathbf{V}) = L(a\mathbf{v}+b\mathbf{w}) = aL(\mathbf{v})+bL(\mathbf{w}).</math>
A linear transformation {{math|''L''}} can be represented by a matrix, which means 

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = {{math|''L'' : '''v''' → [''L'']'''v'''}},}}

where {{math|[''L'']}} is an {{math|''n''×''n''}} matrix.

A linear transformation is a rigid transformation if it satisfies the condition,
<math display="block">d([L]\mathbf{v}, [L]\mathbf{w})^2 = d(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})^2,</math>
that is
<math display="block">d([L]\mathbf{v}, [L]\mathbf{w})^2=([L]\mathbf{v}-[L]\mathbf{w})\cdot([L]\mathbf{v}-[L]\mathbf{w}) =([L](\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w}))\cdot([L](\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w})).</math>
Now use the fact that the scalar product of two vectors '''v'''.'''w''' can be written as the matrix operation {{math|'''v'''<sup>T</sup>'''w'''}}, where the T denotes the matrix transpose, we have
<math display="block">d([L]\mathbf{v}, [L]\mathbf{w})^2 = (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w})^\mathsf{T} [L]^\mathsf{T} [L](\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w}).</math>
Thus, the linear transformation ''L'' is rigid if its matrix satisfies the condition
<math display="block">[L]^\mathsf{T} [L]=[I], </math>
where {{math|[''I'']}} is the identity matrix.  Matrices that satisfy this condition are called ''orthogonal matrices.''  This condition actually requires the columns of these matrices to be orthogonal unit vectors.

Matrices that satisfy this condition form a mathematical [[group (mathematics)|group]] under the operation of matrix multiplication called the ''orthogonal group of n×n matrices'' and denoted {{math|''O''(''n'')}}.

Compute the determinant of the condition for an [[orthogonal matrix]] to obtain
<math display="block"> \det\left([L]^\mathsf{T} [L]\right) = \det[L]^2 = \det[I] = 1,</math>
which shows that the matrix {{math|[''L'']}} can have a determinant of either +1 or −1.  Orthogonal matrices with determinant −1 are reflections, and those with determinant +1 are rotations.  Notice that the set of orthogonal matrices can be viewed as consisting of two manifolds in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''×''n''</sup>}} separated by the set of singular matrices.

The set of rotation matrices is called the ''special orthogonal group,'' and denoted {{math|SO(''n'')}}.  It is an example of a [[Lie group]] because it has the structure of a manifold.
